title: Life Skills Shorts · Episode 1
chapters: Buying big things without the debt trap
Cutting your power and water bills

units.t: Life Skills Shorts. Episode one.
In this episode: Building a better sleep routine, Buying big things without the debt trap, Cutting your power and water bills and Reading your payslip.
Part one. Building a better sleep routine.
Good sleep is less about a magic pill and more about a handful of habits done consistently.
Here is a practical routine you can start tonight.
Anchor your wake time.
Many people try to fix bad sleep by going to bed earlier, then lie awake staring at the ceiling.
A better starting point is the other end of the night.
Your body clock, the circadian rhythm, runs on a cycle of roughly 24 hours and is set largely by when you wake and see light.
Choose a wake time you can keep seven days a week, within about half an hour, weekends included.
Big Saturday sleep-ins shift your clock later, which is part of why Monday mornings feel brutal.
Get outside within an hour of waking, even on a cloudy day.
It is a far stronger signal than indoor lighting.
In the evening, dim the house lights and lower screen brightness.
Caffeine, alcohol and dinner.
That 3 pm flat white may feel harmless, but caffeine stays in your system for several hours, and for some people much longer.
It blocks the receptors for adenosine, a chemical that builds up while you are awake and makes you feel sleepy.
A common suggestion is to have your last caffeine around midday or early afternoon, and to watch for hidden sources such as energy drinks, cola, some teas and dark chocolate.
Alcohol is trickier because it can make you drowsy at first.
Later in the night it tends to disrupt sleep, causing lighter, more broken rest and more trips to the bathroom.
Heavy meals close to bedtime can also cause discomfort, so eat dinner a few hours before bed.
Prepare the night.
Children have bedtime routines for good reason, and adults benefit from the same idea.
For the last half hour to an hour, do a few calm things in roughly the same order, such as a warm shower, setting out tomorrow's clothes, reading a paper book and slow breathing.
Keep work emails and gripping news out of this window.
If worries race, write tomorrow's to-do list first.
Then make the bedroom cool, dark and quiet.
In hot Australian summers, a fan, air conditioning or lighter bedding helps, and block-out curtains or an eye mask cut street light and early dawn.
Check that your mattress and pillow still support you.
Charge your phone outside the room and use a cheap alarm clock instead.
If you cannot sleep.
Lying in bed for an hour willing yourself to sleep can teach your brain to link bed with frustration.
Sleep specialists often suggest a different approach.
If you have been awake for what feels like twenty minutes or so, without clock watching, get up and go to another dim room.
Do something quiet and boring, such as reading or folding washing, and return to bed only when you feel sleepy.
Repeat if needed.
It feels counterintuitive, but over time it rebuilds the link between bed and sleep.
Avoid checking the time repeatedly, which tends to increase anxiety.
Keep naps short, ideally under half an hour and before mid afternoon, so they do not steal sleep from the night.
When to get help.
Most adults are thought to need roughly seven to nine hours of sleep, though individuals vary.
Occasional bad nights are normal, but persistent trouble is worth taking seriously.

See your GP if poor sleep lasts for weeks and affects your daytime life, if a partner notices loud snoring, pauses in breathing or gasping, if you feel very sleepy during the day, especially while driving, or if you have strong urges to move your legs at night.
These can point to treatable sleep conditions.
Effective help exists, including a structured talking therapy for insomnia known as CBT-I. The Sleep Health Foundation and healthdirect have reliable information.
This lesson is general information, not medical advice.
The key idea: A fixed wake time and morning light are the strongest tools for setting your body clock.
Part two. Buying big things without the debt trap.
A new fridge, a laptop, a couch: big purchases often come with a tempting offer to pay later.
Here is how buy now pay later, interest-free deals and rent-to-own really work, and a better way to buy.
How pay-later works.
At checkout, a friendly line appears: four easy payments, no interest.
A thousand-dollar purchase suddenly looks like a few hundred.
That shift in feeling is the point.
Splitting a cost makes it easier to say yes, and research suggests people tend to spend more when paying feels less painful.
Buy now pay later typically means four payments over about six weeks, the first upfront.
Many charge no interest, earning money from retailers' fees and customers' late or account fees.
Since mid-2025, BNPL has been regulated as credit, so providers need a credit licence and must check the product isn't unsuitable for you.
The risks are several plans across providers, missed-payment fees and credit report problems.
This is general information, not financial advice.
Interest-free fine print.
Furniture and electronics stores often advertise long interest-free periods, perhaps a year or more, through a store card or finance partner.
These can be useful if you pay the full amount within the period.
The trap is what happens if you don't.
Any remaining balance usually starts attracting a high rate, often similar to a credit card.
Many of these products also charge a monthly account fee, and some an establishment fee, so the deal isn't truly free.
The account may stay open for future purchases.
Before signing, ask three questions: what is the rate after the interest-free period, what are the fees, and what is the minimum repayment?
Rent-to-own leases.
Some businesses offer appliances, furniture or electronics on a weekly lease, sometimes promoted to people on Centrelink payments with deductions taken straight from their payments.
These leases can cost much more than the retail price, and at the end you may not own the item.
ASIC has repeatedly warned about the high cost of some leases.
If you need an essential like a fridge or washing machine and can't afford it, look at alternatives first.
The No Interest Loan Scheme, run by Good Shepherd with community partners, offers loans for essential goods to eligible people on low incomes, with no interest or fees.
Services Australia may also offer an advance payment if you receive certain payments.
Pause and find the total.
A simple habit stops most regretful purchases: wait.
For anything over an amount you choose, perhaps a few hundred dollars, give yourself 48 hours, or a week for bigger items.
If you still want it, it's probably a considered decision rather than an impulse.
Next, work out the total cost, not the instalment.
Add up every payment and fee if you use credit.
Then ask a blunt question: if I had to pay the full price today from my own money, would I still buy it?
If not, the payment plan is making the decision for you.
Check that your existing repayments plus this one still leave room for rent, bills and food.
Save first, buy smarter.
The cheapest way to buy something big is usually to save first.
A sinking fund is money set aside regularly for a known future cost, such as a laptop, car registration or a replacement fridge.
Divide the expected price by the pay cycles until you need it, and automate a transfer into a separate account on payday.
You earn a little interest instead of paying it, and cash can give you bargaining power.
Ask politely whether paying upfront gets a better price.
Compare prices across retailers, and be wary of 'sale' prices that aren't real bargains.
Consider quality secondhand goods.
New goods come with automatic consumer guarantees under the Australian Consumer Law, which can matter more than an extended warranty.
The key idea: Pay-later offers make big prices feel small, and the risks come from stacking plans and missing payments.
Part three. Cutting your power and water bills.
Your energy bill is a story about heat: heating rooms, heating water and keeping food cold.
Read it properly and you can find real savings without living in the dark.
Read your bill.
Look past the total on your electricity bill.
The daily supply charge is a fixed amount you pay just to be connected.
The usage charge is a price per kilowatt hour, kWh, the unit your meter counts.
One kWh is a 1,000 watt appliance running for an hour.
Time of use plans charge more at peak times.
Watch your average daily use as you make changes.
People often start by unplugging phone chargers, which is like skipping a mint while buying a new car.
In most Australian homes, heating and cooling are the biggest users, then water heating, then fridges, dryers and pool pumps.
To find big users, multiply wattage by hours.
A 2,400 watt heater running five hours a night uses 12 kilowatt hours.
Heating and cooling smarter.
A reverse cycle air conditioner is a heat pump.
Rather than turning electricity directly into heat, it moves heat from outside to inside.
It can deliver several units of heat for each unit of electricity, which typically makes it far cheaper to run than a plug-in bar or fan heater.
Thermostat settings matter too.
Australian energy agencies commonly suggest around 18 to 20 degrees in winter and 25 to 27 in summer, and each extra degree adds noticeably to running costs.
Heat or cool only the rooms you use.
Seal draughts around doors and windows with weather strips and door snakes.
Close curtains on winter nights, and block summer sun with external shading, which works better than internal blinds.
Hot water, fridge, standby.
Every hot shower costs you twice: once for the water and again to heat it.
A showerhead with a good Water Efficiency Labelling and Standards, WELS, star rating uses less hot water, and cutting a shower by a couple of minutes adds up over a year.
Fix dripping hot taps quickly and wash clothes in cold water.
Your fridge runs all day, so keep it at around 3 to 4 degrees and the freezer around minus 18.
Check the door seals by closing the door on a sheet of paper to see if it holds, and leave space behind for air.
An old second fridge in the garage can be surprisingly expensive to run.
Walk through your home at night and count the glowing standby lights.
Switch off consoles and spare devices at the wall.
Saving water.
A toilet with a slow leak into the bowl can waste a large amount of water without anyone noticing.
Test yours by adding a few drops of food colouring to the cistern and waiting about 15 minutes without flushing.
If colour appears in the bowl, the cistern is leaking and needs repair.
Most plumbing repairs need a licensed plumber.
Use the half flush button where you have one.
Run dishwashers and washing machines only when full, and look for good WELS star ratings when buying them.
Outside, water the garden early in the morning or in the evening so less is lost to evaporation, and use mulch to keep soil moist.
Check local water restrictions and rebates.
Buy smart, shop around.
The Energy Rating Label shows a star rating and an estimated yearly energy use in kWh, the best number for comparing models of a similar size.
A cheaper appliance with a poor rating can cost more over its life than a pricier efficient one.
Many households stay on the same plan for years and pay more than they need to.
Compare plans every year or so.
The government's Energy Made Easy website, energymadeeasy.
gov.
au, compares offers in most states and territories, and Victoria has its own Victorian Energy Compare site.
Ask your retailer if they have a better plan.
If you hold a pension, health care or other concession card, ask about energy concessions.
If you are struggling to pay, contact your retailer early about hardship programs.
This is general information only.
The key idea: Bills combine a daily supply charge with a price per kilowatt hour, and heating, cooling and hot water are the big users.
Part four. Reading your payslip.
That little document on payday tells you whether you are being paid correctly.
Most people never really read it.
Here is how.
Why your payslip matters.
Imagine working the same Saturday shifts for a year, only to discover your weekend penalty rate was never applied.
Underpayment is more common than many people realise, and it is not always deliberate.
Payroll errors, wrong award classifications and outdated rates all happen, and your payslip is where they show up first.
In Australia, employers generally must give employees a payslip within one working day of payday, on paper or electronically.
Reading it takes two minutes each pay and can save you hundreds or thousands of dollars.
This is general information, not legal or financial advice.
The Fair Work Ombudsman, fairwork.
gov.
au, is the official place to check your situation.
What must be on it.
A compliant payslip names your employer, including their ABN, and names you.
It shows the pay period and the date you were paid.
Gross pay is your total before tax.
Net pay is what lands in your bank account.
It should also list deductions such as tax or salary sacrifice, plus any bonuses, loadings, allowances or penalty rates.
If you are paid by the hour, it shows your hourly rate and the hours paid at that rate.
It shows the superannuation your employer is paying and the fund it is going to.
If any of this is missing, politely ask your payroll team why.
Tax and super.
Under the pay as you go system, your employer withholds tax and sends it to the Australian Taxation Office.
The amount depends on your earnings, how often you are paid and your tax file number declaration.
Claim the tax-free threshold from one employer only; claiming it in two jobs can leave you with a bill at tax time.
Super is paid on top of your wages.
The super guarantee is a percentage of your ordinary time earnings, 12 per cent since 1 July 2025; the ATO website lists the current rate.
Since 1 July 2026, employers must pay super each payday, and it should reach your fund within seven business days.
A payslip only shows what your employer says it paid, so check your fund's app or myGov regularly.
Rates, penalties and awards.
Many Australian workers are covered by a modern award, a legal document that sets minimum pay and conditions for an industry or occupation.
Others are covered by an enterprise agreement negotiated at their workplace.
These set your minimum base rate and extras such as casual loading, overtime and penalty rates for evenings, weekends and public holidays.
To check yours, use the Fair Work Ombudsman's pay calculator or download your award's pay guide.
You will need your award, your classification level and whether you are full time, part time or casual.
Minimum rates are usually reviewed each year, with changes commonly starting from the first full pay period on or after 1 July.
A rate that was right last year might be wrong now.
Routine and fixing errors.
Keep a note of your hours each week, including start and finish times and breaks.
When your payslip arrives, compare the hours with your record and check that each type, such as overtime or Sunday work, has the right rate.
Glance at the year to date totals and your leave balance.
Save every payslip as a PDF in one folder, because records are your best evidence.
If something looks wrong, write to your manager or payroll.
Say what you noticed, what you believe is correct and how you worked it out, and keep a copy.
If it is not fixed, the Fair Work Ombudsman offers free help, and the ATO handles unpaid super.
Time limits apply to recovering wages, so act early.
Employers must not punish you for raising a genuine concern.
The key idea: Your payslip is your best everyday check that you are being paid what you are owed.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why is a steady wake time a better starting point than an earlier bedtime?
Answer. It anchors your body clock, set by waking and light.
Question two. Since mid-2025, how is buy now pay later regulated in Australia?
Answer. As a form of credit requiring a licence.
Question three. Which usually uses the most energy in an Australian home?
Answer. Heating and cooling.
Question four. Why is it worth reading your payslip every pay?
Answer. It is where pay errors, such as a missing penalty rate, show up first.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
